title: A Handful of Great Decisions Drown Out All of the Bad Ones
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Citing Warren Buffett's observation that a handful of great investment decisions have outweighed decades of mediocre ones at Berkshire Hathaway, this piece argues that lifetime success hinges on getting a few pivotal decisions right rather than avoiding all bad ones. The author's central claim is that people decisions — who to trust, partner with, hire, and spend time with — matter more than the 'meaty' strategic decisions leaders usually treat as most consequential. The piece closes by pointing to end-of-life regret patterns as evidence that people-related choices carry the heaviest long-term weight.
points: A small number of genuinely great decisions can outweigh a much larger number of mediocre or bad ones over a career or lifetime.
People decisions — who you trust, hire, partner with, and spend time with — carry more long-term weight than strategic decisions about products, capital, or M&A.
Leaders' biggest end-of-life regrets tend to center on misplaced trust in people, not on failed investments or strategic bets.
The practical implication is to focus disproportionate care on 'people decisions' since they compound the most over time.
quotes: Legendary investor Warren Buffett claims that investment decisions at his firm Berkshire Hathaway have been no better than so-so over nearly six decades.
It’s not how many bad decisions we make, but how many good ones that change the complexion of our existence.
The most important decisions we make are about the people we trust, partner with, hire, and spend time with.
They regret trusting someone they shouldn’t have or having gotten involved in a partnership that was wrong for them.
The purpose of relationship is not to have another who might complete you, but to have another with whom you might share your completeness.
